options.content: A copy of only the files changed since the last backup
options.rationale: Correct: incrementals copy just the changes.

options.content: A copy of every selected file each time it runs
options.rationale: That is a full backup.

options.content: A copy kept in a different building from the original
options.rationale: That describes off-site storage, not a backup method.

options.content: A copy of old files moved off the main system for storage
options.rationale: That is archiving.

explanation: An incremental backup copies only the files that have changed since the previous backup.

stem: Why should at least one backup be kept **off-site**?

options.content: So it survives a fire, flood or theft at the main site
options.rationale: Correct: an on-site copy can be lost in the same disaster.

options.content: So that backups run faster than they would on-site
options.rationale: Off-site copies are usually slower to make and fetch.

options.content: So that no password is needed to restore the data
options.rationale: Off-site backups should still be protected.

options.content: So that the original files never need to be saved
options.rationale: Originals are still saved; backups are extra copies.

explanation: A disaster that destroys the original is likely to destroy any backup in the same building too.

stem: Which is an advantage of a **full** backup compared with an incremental backup?

options.content: It takes less time to make each backup
options.rationale: Full backups take the longest to make.

options.content: It uses less storage space on the backup media
options.rationale: Full backups use the most storage.

options.content: It copies only the files that have just changed
options.rationale: That describes an incremental backup.

options.content: Data can be restored from a single backup set
options.rationale: Correct: no chain of incrementals is needed.

explanation: A full backup contains everything, so restoring needs only that one set.

stem: Which item belongs in a **disaster recovery plan**?

options.content: The company's advertising budget for next year
options.rationale: Marketing plans are not part of disaster recovery.

options.content: The colour scheme of the company website
options.rationale: This has nothing to do with recovering from a disaster.

options.content: A list of the staff's favourite websites at work
options.rationale: Not relevant to recovery.

options.content: The steps and people responsible for restoring systems
options.rationale: Correct: recovery procedures and roles are central to the plan.

explanation: A disaster recovery plan includes risks, backup policy, recovery procedures, responsibilities, alternative arrangements and testing.

stem: Tatenda accidentally deletes a folder and empties the recycle bin. Why should he stop using the disk before running file recovery software?

options.content: Recovery software only works on a disk that is completely full
options.rationale: Recovery works on any disk; fullness is not required.

options.content: Using the disk will automatically restore the files from a backup
options.rationale: No backup is restored without being asked.

options.content: New data could overwrite the space where the deleted files still are
options.rationale: Correct: deleted data stays until its space is reused.

options.content: The operating system wipes deleted files after ten minutes
options.rationale: Files are not wiped on a timer.

explanation: Deleting usually only marks the space as free. Recovery software can rebuild the files unless new data has overwritten them.
hints: What happens to the free space after a file is deleted?

stem: A company's computers are hit by ransomware that encrypts every connected drive. Which backup is **most likely** to be usable?

options.content: An external disk left permanently plugged into the server
options.rationale: A connected disk is likely to be encrypted too.

options.content: A second folder on the same hard disk
options.rationale: This is encrypted along with the original.

options.content: A cloud or off-site copy not connected at the time
options.rationale: Correct: a disconnected copy cannot be encrypted by the ransomware.

options.content: The recycle bin on the infected computer
options.rationale: The recycle bin is on the infected disk.

explanation: Backups kept off-site or disconnected cannot be reached by malware on the network, so they survive.
hints: Ransomware may encrypt any drive connected to the computer.

stem: A small clinic changes about 2% of its data each day. Which backup strategy is **most** suitable?

options.content: A full backup once a year to a disk kept in the reception desk
options.rationale: Too infrequent, and stored on-site where it can be lost.

options.content: Weekly full and daily incremental backups, with a copy in the cloud
options.rationale: Correct: fast daily backups, little storage, and an off-site copy.

options.content: Daily full backups to a second folder on the same computer
options.rationale: Slow, wasteful and lost if the disk fails.

options.content: No backups, because the data changes so little each day
options.rationale: Even small daily changes would be lost after a failure.

explanation: With little daily change, incrementals are quick and small; a weekly full backup keeps restores manageable; the cloud copy is off-site.
hints: Balance backup time, storage and safety.

stem: To restore data from incremental backups you need the last full backup and every incremental backup made after it.
explanation: True. Each incremental holds only the changes since the previous backup, so the whole chain is needed.

stem: Once backups are scheduled, there is no need to test them.
explanation: False. Backups should be tested by restoring sample files; a backup that cannot be restored is useless.

stem: Match each backup location to a disadvantage.

left.content: External disk on the same desk

right.content: Takes time to fetch when a restore is needed
Lost in the same fire or theft as the computer

explanation: On-site copies share the same risks; cloud needs internet; off-site disks are slow to fetch.

stem: Match each problem to the most suitable recovery tool.

left.content: A file was deleted an hour ago and the bin has not been emptied
A new driver has made the computer unstable
The server's disk has failed completely
A deleted photo is needed and there is no backup

right.content: Restore the backup onto a new disk
Restore it from the recycle bin
Roll back to a system restore point

explanation: Recycle bin for recent deletions; restore point for system changes; backup for failed disks; recovery software when no backup exists.

stem: A full backup is made every Sunday night and an incremental backup every other night. The server fails on Friday afternoon, before Friday's backup. Complete the restore plan.

payload.template: First restore the full backup from {{blank:a}}, then the incremental backups from Monday to {{blank:b}}. In total, {{blank:c}} backup sets are restored.

explanation: Restore Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday: 5 sets (1 full + 4 incremental).
hints: Start from the last full backup.

stem: A business's files total 40 GB. About 3 GB changes each day. It makes one full backup each week and an incremental backup on each of the other six days. How many GB of backup storage does one week need?
explanation: 40 + 6 × 3 = 58 GB (seven full backups would need 280 GB).
workedSolution:
1. Full backup: 40 GB.
2. Six incrementals: 6 × 3 = 18 GB.
3. Total: 40 + 18 = 58 GB.
hints: One full backup plus six incrementals.

stem: State **four** different causes of data loss.

points.description: Theft / fire / flood / power surge or cut

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A hard disk crash; ransomware encrypting the files; a user deleting the wrong folder; a fire destroying the office.

explanation: Data can be lost through hardware failure, malware, human error, theft and natural or electrical disasters.
hints: Think of hardware, people, malware and nature.

stem: Recommend a backup strategy for a secondary school's administration office and justify each part.

points.description: Method: e.g. weekly full plus daily incremental, so backups are quick but restores manageable
Frequency / timing: automatic, every night when the office is closed
Location: a copy off-site or in the cloud (encrypted), so a fire or theft does not destroy it
Testing: restore sample files regularly to prove the backups work

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Run a full backup every Friday night and an incremental backup every other night, automatically, so little work is lost. Keep an encrypted copy in a cloud backup service so it survives a fire or burglary. Each month, restore a sample folder to prove the backups work.

explanation: A strong answer covers method, frequency, location and testing, each with a reason.
hints: What, when, where, and how it is checked.

stem: Masvingo Motor Spares (fictional) makes a full backup every Saturday night and an incremental backup on the other nights, to an external disk kept beside the server.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: The server fails on Wednesday morning. How many backup sets must be restored?
parts.workedSolution:
1. Last full backup: Saturday.
2. Incrementals after it: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday.
3. Total: 4.

parts.label: (b)

options.content: Saturday
options.rationale: That is the full backup, restored first.

options.content: Tuesday
options.rationale: Correct: the most recent incremental is restored last.

options.content: Wednesday
options.rationale: No backup had been made on the day of failure.

options.content: Sunday
options.rationale: This is the first incremental, not the last.

parts.explanation: Incrementals are restored oldest first, ending with Tuesday.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why keeping the backup disk beside the server is a weakness, and suggest an improvement.

points.description: Fire, flood or theft would destroy / remove the backup together with the server
Keep a copy off-site or in the cloud (encrypted)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A fire or burglary in the server room would destroy both the server and the backup. A second, encrypted copy should be kept in the cloud or taken off-site.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** items, other than the backup schedule, that the shop's disaster recovery plan should contain.

points.description: One item (e.g. risk assessment / recovery procedures / roles and contacts)
A second item (e.g. alternative equipment or site / testing and review / critical systems list)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Step-by-step recovery procedures, and the names and phone numbers of the people responsible for each task.

hints: Count the full backup and each incremental after it.

stem: Thandeka runs a small accounting practice in Bulawayo with five computers. Power cuts are frequent and the internet connection is sometimes slow.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Compare an on-site external disk with a cloud backup service for the practice, giving **two** advantages of each.

points.description: External disk: fast to back up and restore
External disk: works without internet / no subscription
Cloud: off-site, survives fire or theft
Cloud: automatic / accessible from anywhere / storage can grow

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An external disk is quick to back up to and restore from, and it works even when the internet is down. A cloud service keeps the data away from the office, so it survives a fire or theft, and it runs automatically and can be reached from anywhere.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the disaster recovery plan must be tested and reviewed regularly.

points.description: Testing shows whether backups can actually be restored / staff know what to do
Reviewing keeps it up to date with new systems, staff, risks and contacts

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Testing proves that the backups really restore and that staff can follow the steps quickly. Reviewing updates the plan when systems, staff or risks change.

explanation: A combination of an on-site disk and an encrypted cloud copy gives speed and safety.
hints: Weigh internet access and cost against safety.
